Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside them, a lender can still require it.

A private flood policy can meet a lender's flood requirement: federally regulated lenders must accept a private policy that meets the federal definition of private flood insurance and covers at least what the loan requires (12 CFR §339.3(c)). Its price is not in FEMA's records.

67.3% of California's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones (not 67.3% of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home).

Every zone starting with A or V is high-risk, including older numbered labels such as A1 to A30 from older flood maps (newer maps use AE for the same kind of area). Policies keep the label they were rated with, so the old labels are counted on their own.

Insured units by the zone each policy is rated in. How this is counted

Not in the NFIP (5 communities here): Coachella; Gustine; Mariposa County; Selma; Trinidad. Federal flood insurance (NFIP) is sold only in communities that take part in the NFIP; in a community that has not joined, has withdrawn or is suspended, no one can buy an NFIP policy.

How much does it cost here?

Typically about $1,053 a year ($88 a month), fees included. Half of homeowners here pay between $738 and $1,277. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $738 · Typical $1,053 · A quarter pay over $1,277 · A tenth pay $1,874 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 101,902 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

Coverage in force: $42.7 billion of building and $10.1 billion of contents coverage across all California policies.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy, but there is no wait if you buy it with a new or refinanced mortgage.

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageNo wait
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Standard homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage; flood insurance is bought separately, through the federal NFIP or a private insurer. Exceptions: no wait if you buy while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage; a one-day wait if a map revision puts the property in a high-risk zone and you buy within 13 months of the revision (44 CFR §61.11). To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a signed proof of loss within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster. If FEMA aid pays to repair a home in a high-risk zone, you must buy and keep flood insurance on it, or you cannot get that aid again after a later flood.

Source: floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

What do floods actually pay out here?

Floods here have led to 53,563 NFIP flood claims and $759.0 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 1995, 2005 and 2023.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 1995 ($115,910,399), 2005 ($91,112,351), 2023 ($64,729,267). Total paid $758,994,896. Totals for the latest two years are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

That is 53,563 claims since 1978 against 173,168 policy units in force today — a cumulative tally spanning ~49 years over a present-day snapshot, not an annual claim rate or a flood probability.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective 1978–2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 48.7% of the 72,211 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 72,211 policies reporting one)48.7%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)89.0%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 33,314 claims paid with a damage figure)4.8%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Source: floodsmart.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Why do sites quote different prices for California?

Because they measure different things. Existing single-family policies here typically cost $1,053 a year, and policies first bought in the past year $1,044; other sites count other policies, years or averages.

MeasureAmountWhat it counts
Typical cost, single-family homes (median)$1,053premium plus fees; the middle policy
Typical premium only$831before the federal fee, reserve fund and surcharge
Typical cost, policies whose term began in 2025$1,04347,417 policies
Typical cost, policies whose term began in 2026$1,06354,485 policies
Typical cost, policies first bought in the past year$1,04411,418 policies, past year
FEMA's full-risk premium (median)$934the price FEMA's model sets for these existing policies
Full-risk premium plus average fees$1,175what these existing policies would cost at FEMA's full price
Average (mean) cost, single-family homes$1,183pulled up by a few expensive policies
Average cost, every policy type$1,423adds condos, rentals and businesses

Condo owners: condo-unit policies are 3.4% of NFIP policy units here. The single-family figures above leave both out; only the every-policy-type average includes them.

All from the NFIP policies in force on July 31, 2026. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

44.8% of policies here pay less than FEMA's full-risk price, so their bills are rising toward it. Median premium $831, full-risk $934 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$831
  • Median full-risk premium$934
  • Pay below full-risk44.8% of 101,902

Yearly cap: Those prices step up toward full-risk each year, limited by the yearly cap. By law a primary home's premium cannot rise more than 18% a year; some policies, such as second homes and businesses, can rise up to 25%. The cap usually does not apply to new policies, and fees and surcharges sit outside it. Bills already at full risk still change with FEMA's yearly rate updates.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies. Data effective July 31, 2026; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Can I pay less?

The usual building deductible here is $1,250 (41.5% of single-family policies). FEMA's ways to lower an NFIP bill: a higher deductible (you pay more of any loss), work that lowers the building's flood risk, and an Elevation Certificate.

Single-family primary homes; the commonest deductibles. Your lender may limit how high you can go.

Only the latest are listed, newest first, one line per disaster; the count covers every flood, hurricane, tropical-storm and coastal-storm declaration FEMA lists here, plus severe-storm declarations whose title names flooding, including emergency declarations. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Disaster Declarations Summaries. Data: declarations through 2024; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $124.8 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $2,733 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved October 25, 2026.

Are these counts complete?

Every record FEMA's download lists was received and counted.

In-force count: 173,168 policy units (from 158,060 API records; condo-association records carry more than one unit). Download check: policies: 158,060 of 158,060 fetched; claims: 53,563 of 53,563 fetched.
